title: A Transparency Checklist for Theory-Driven Work in Psychology
description: This expansion pack extends the RESQUE publication core set (see http://www.resque.info) with a structured transparency checklist for theory-driven psychological research. It covers the description and formalization of theories, evaluation through simulations, mathematical derivations, and empirical tests, and comparisons among competing theories or models. Filter questions present only the checklist items relevant to the work being reported.

elements.title: Theory-guided research and theory development

options.text: This research was mainly descriptive / exploratory, without a clear theoretical rationale
This research was theoretically motivated and (further) developed and/or evaluated at least one (part of a) theory
Cannot answer the question

elements.info:
These criteria apply not only to purely theoretical work but also to original empirical work that incorporates theoretical reasoning in generating its hypotheses. Thus, if the paper states any theoretically derived hypotheses or the like, you should choose the second option here.

Orienting Question:
Was there a theoretical motivation for conducting this research?
The following items assess how transparently a theory is described, formalized, evaluated, and compared.

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …contains an explicit verbal description of at least one phenomenon to be explained by the developed / tested theory.

elements.info:
Phenomena are stable features of the world that may constitute the targets of scientific explanation. In psychology, such features are typically inferred from robust patterns of observations (i.e., observations that are made repeatedly and through the use of different procedures).

Orienting Question:
Does it become clear what the theory aims to explain?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …provides a working definition for all central concepts used in the theory or provides a clear reference to a previous definition of the concept.

elements.info:
A concept is an abstract idea used to describe, differentiate, or reason about certain aspects of the world. Concepts might not always have an accepted definition. Yet, it is important to provide a working definition and to clearly communicate how the concept is used / understood in the context of the theory.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear what the concepts mentioned in the theory are about?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …defines (in verbal form) the central relationships among the concepts used in the theory or provides a clear reference to a previous definition of this relationship.

elements.info:
Verbal definitions are still required even if concepts and their relations are expressed in a formalized way (e.g., in a formula). While formalizations are inherently more precise, verbal expressions are still necessary for others to properly understand the content of the formalization.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear how the concepts mentioned in the theory are related to each other?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …describes a mechanism explaining how the relevant phenomena arise.

elements.info:
A mechanism is the causal or functional pathway through which entities, processes, and their organization give rise to a phenomenon.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear how the theory explains the phenomenon?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …discusses the intended scope of the theory and, where possible, specifies known boundary conditions or limitations of its applicability.

elements.info:
This concerns assumptions about generality (e.g., subject and stimulus population characteristics) as well as simplifying assumptions. When building on an existing theory, a clear reference to a prior scope statement can be sufficient if the scope is unchanged.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear under which conditions / in which situations the theory is applicable?

elements.title: Does the paper formalize (parts of) the theory in a formal model?

options.text: No
Yes

elements.info:
That is, the properties of and the connections among the elements of (a part of) the theory are expressed through formal means, such as mathematical equations, algorithms, or logical propositions.

It should be noted that a formal model specifies a data generating process that enables the running of simulations. This is different from a statistical model, which mainly aims to describe data instead of explaining its generating process.

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …specifies any auxiliary assumption that had to be added to enable the translation of the verbal theory into a formal model.

elements.info:
An auxiliary assumption is any assumption or decision not directly implied by the theory but introduced for purposes such as formalization, simulation, prediction, or empirical testing.

Orienting Question:
Are modelling decisions that are not directly implied by the theory made explicit?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …lists all elements of the formal model and defines them by connecting them to their corresponding elements of the verbal theory (if available). If an element of the model represents an auxiliary assumption, this is made explicit.

elements.info:
Elements of the formal model subsume all the variables, parameters, constants, functions, operators, and auxiliary assumptions that were used to arrive at a specific formalization of a theory.

Specifying all the elements of a formal model can also be achieved using a Table or an Appendix. Common mathematical operators can be exempt from this requirement.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear what each element in the formal model is supposed to represent?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …specifies the basic mathematical properties of all elements of the formal model (e.g., scalar vs. matrix, dimensionality, etc.).

elements.info:
Even if all elements of the formal model have a narrative definition, their mathematical properties might be unclear (e.g., is parameter B a constant, a vector, or a two-dimensional matrix?).

This can also be ensured by referring to an established standard notation.

Orienting Question:
Are the (mathematical) properties for each element of the model clear?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …specifies constraints on the possible values for all elements of the formal model (e.g., upper and lower bounds, scale level, prior distributions). If a parameter has no assumed constraints/scale, this is made explicit.

elements.info:
These constraints may be directly implied by the theory, introduced through auxiliary assumptions, or based on empirical observations.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear which values each element in the model can possibly take?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …states whether the model is structurally identifiable — that is, whether distinct parameter values produce distinct patterns of predictions — or defines constraints under which identifiability can be achieved. If identifiability does not apply to the model or was not assessed, this is stated explicitly.

elements.info:
Structural identifiability is a property of the model, not of any single element. It concerns whether the model’s parameters can, in principle, be distinguished from the full pattern of predictions the model generates. A model is structurally identifiable when no two distinct parameter configurations produce the same predicted pattern across all of the model’s outputs.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of the model’s structural identifiability?

elements.title: Did you evaluate (a part of) this theory / model?

options.text: No
Yes, by using simulations and / or mathematical derivations
Yes, by comparing its predictions against empirical observations
Yes, by both simulations / mathematical derivations AND empirical observations

elements.info:
Tests by simulation always require the evaluated theory to be formalized. Empirical tests can also be applied to purely narrative theories. Both may apply to the same paper.

Orienting Question:
Was the theory evaluated not at all, via simulations / mathematical derivations, via empirical data, or both?

elements.title: The simulation part of the paper …

options.text: …specifies any additional *auxiliary assumption* that had to be added for the purpose of running the simulation (e.g., restriction of parameter ranges, fixed parameters, number of iterations, etc.).

elements.info:
An auxiliary assumption is any assumption or decision not directly implied by the theory but introduced for purposes such as formalization, simulation, prediction, or empirical testing.

Orienting Question:
Are decisions that are not implied by the theory / model made explicit?

elements.title: The simulation part of the paper …

options.text: …provides an assessment of how well the model *reproduces the data patterns* indicative of the phenomena to be explained.

elements.info:
Such an assessment should always cover whether the model reproduces the data pattern qualitatively but may also cover aspects of quantitative fit, depending on how narrowly the phenomena are defined.

Orienting Question:
Did the work attempt to reproduce the data pattern indicative of the phenomenon that is to be explained?

elements.title: The simulation part of the paper …

options.text:
…provides an assessment of the *robustness* of the simulation results by, for example, using any of the following or similarly appropriate methods:
  • Varying auxiliary assumptions that could meaningfully affect the results and testing whether the model's success in reproducing the data pattern indicative of the relevant phenomena is dependent on these assumptions.
  • Exploring the simulation results across a range of justifiable parameter values to characterize the plausible parameter space.

elements.info:
In the best case, the model’s success in reproducing the data pattern indicative of the relevant phenomena should not depend on the auxiliary assumptions but only on the core assumptions.

Orienting Question:
Does the paper implement one of these (or similar) practices to test the robustness of the simulation results?

elements.title: The simulation part of the paper …

options.text: …provides an assessment of whether the *relevant phenomena arise from the theory’s mechanism(s)* by, for example, changing (i.e., deleting or replacing) the mechanism(s) to test whether the relevant phenomena fail to emerge.

elements.info:
This concerns the empirical relevance of the theory’s mechanism: do the relevant phenomena emerge as a consequence of the core theoretical assumptions, or is it a byproduct of auxiliary assumptions? Altering or removing the mechanism(s) should ideally lead to a failure in reproducing the relevant phenomena.

Orienting Question:
Does the paper assess whether relevant phenomena emerge from the mechanism(s) postulated by the theory/model?

elements.title: The simulation part of the paper …

options.text: …contains an explicit *discussion* as to what the results of the simulation mean for the theory that was tested (e.g., support, refutation, limitation of scope, adding or subtracting theory elements), also considering the plausibility of auxiliary assumptions that had been added in the process.

elements.info:
A single test often cannot definitively refute a theory because auxiliary assumptions are always involved; the plausibility of these assumptions should therefore be discussed alongside the simulation outcome.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of what the simulation results imply for the theory that was tested?

elements.title: The empirical part of the paper …

options.text: …describes how each element in the theory that is relevant to the current test was *operationalized* (i.e., measured, estimated, fixed, or manipulated) in an experimental design.

elements.info:
Operationalization is the process of specifying how (some of) the elements of a theory/formal model are measured, manipulated, or estimated to make the theory testable.

Orienting Question:
Is it clear how each element of the theory was operationalized?

elements.title: The empirical part of the paper …

options.text: …makes transparent how *predictions were derived from the theory*, either by providing a rationale of how the predictions logically follow from the verbal theory, or by formally deriving the predictions from a formal model.

elements.info:
Orienting Question:
Is it clear how the tested predictions follow from the theory?

elements.title: The empirical part of the paper …

options.text: …provides an assessment of how *consistent* the theory’s / model’s predictions are with the observed empirical data.

elements.info:
Orienting Question:
Is there an evaluation of how consistent the empirical observations are with the theoretical predictions?

elements.title: The empirical part of the paper …

options.text: …provides a discussion of how *informative* the empirical test was for evaluating the theory. That is, how narrowly the theory constrained the space of plausible observations as opposed to being compatible with a wide range of other plausible observations.

elements.info:
A close fit between theory and data provides strong support only if the theory could have failed, i.e. if it forbids a substantial range of otherwise plausible observations. A theory compatible with almost any result gains little support from a confirming observation. Thus, the more observations the theory rules out, the more informative the test.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of whether the theory forbids a substantial range of otherwise plausible observations?

elements.title: The empirical part of the paper …

options.text: …contains an explicit discussion as to *what the empirical results mean for the theory* that was tested (e.g., support, refutation, limitation of scope, adding or subtracting theory elements), considering the plausibility of auxiliary assumptions that had been added in the process.

elements.info:
Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of what the empirical results imply for the theory that was tested?

elements.title: Did you compare the tested theory/model to other theories/models?

options.text: No
Yes

elements.info: These items only apply when the paper explicitly compares two or more theories / models.

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …provides a comparison of each theory’s / model’s predictive accuracy, i.e., how well they reproduce the data pattern indicative of the phenomena of interest.

elements.info:
Ideally, predictive accuracy should be assessed out-of-sample, that is, on a data set that was not used to construct and/or fit the theory/model.

Orienting Question:
Is there a comparison of the predictive accuracy of all of the compared theories’ / models’ predictions?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …provides a comparison of how narrowly each theory / model constrains the space of plausible observations as opposed to being consistent with a wide range of other plausible observations.

elements.info:
Two theories / models may reproduce the target phenomenon equally well but differ in how much else they permit. A theory that predicts the data pattern indicative of the relevant phenomena while ruling out more alternative observations is better supported when its prediction holds compared to a theory that is also consistent with other alternative observations.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of how narrowly each theory / model constrains the predictive space?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …provides a comparison of each theory’s / model’s explanatory breadth, i.e., the range of other relevant phenomena each theory / model can account for.

elements.info:
Two theories / models can account for a different number of phenomena. A theory / model that accounts for more phenomena than another theory / model, has higher explanatory breadth and should be preferred. Note that this point is different from C2, which is about how precisely each of these phenomena is predicted.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of the explanatory breadth of the theories / models?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …provides a comparison of each theory’s / model’s *parsimony*, i.e., its simplicity in explaining the relevant phenomena.

elements.info:
Theories / models with fewer parameters that nevertheless explain all the phenomena of interest should be preferred over theories / models with more parameters that explain the same number of phenomena.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of the parsimony of the theories / models?

elements.title: The paper …

options.text: …explicitly discusses the trade-off between each theory’s / model’s predictive accuracy, precision, explanatory breadth, and parsimony.

elements.info:
Being inferior to another theory / model in one regard may be offset by being superior in another. For instance, if a theory / model has one parameter more than another but explains many more phenomena, it may be plausible to prefer the less parsimonious over the more parsimonious theory / model.

Orienting Question:
Is there a discussion of the trade-off between each theory’s / model’s characteristics?
